newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-ALL'S WELL EXCEPT LOUD MUSIC, PINWHEELS - COMMISSIONER.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-ALL'S WELL EXCEPT LOUD MUSIC, PINWHEELS - COMMISSIONER.

text.p: With no labour disputes to address, NBA Commissioner David Stern was free to discuss violence, racial issues, 3-point shooting and loud music in his annual Finals news conference Monday.

Stern presented the 1996-97 NBA Sportsmanship Award to Terrell Brandon and said that while the Cleveland Cavaliers point guard's professionalism and fine character were "more representative" of the NBA than "the tabloids" would indicate, "it doesn't seem to make the copy that other exploits might."

The league has had several violent incidents recently, and Stern, addressing the media at the Chicago Bulls' United Centre arena, expressed complete support for the rule that automatically suspends players who come off the bench and onto the court during an altercation.

The rule helped send the New York Knicks down to defeat in their Eastern Conference semifinal with the Miami Heat after leading three games to one. Centre Patrick Ewing said he felt Stern had "robbed" him of a shot at the title by suspending him and three teammates who came off the bench.
Asked if he had spoken to Ewing since then, Stern said, somewhat mysteriously: "We have communicated with each other."
Asked if he would like to share that communication, Stern said: "No."

Deputy Commissioner Russ Granik noted that, "for the first time in three or four years we're not here talking about whether we might have a work stoppage" and presented some possible changes in the rules of the actual game.

These included moving the 3-point line back to the old 23 feet, 9 inches (7.24 metres) from its current 22 feet (6.71 metres), reviewing blocking and charging definitions and fine-tuning illegal defence rules.
Representatives from all teams were scheduled Tuesday to discuss a special rules panel's findings and send recommendations to the league Board of Governors in the next month, Granik said.
"I'll be surprised if there aren't some changes to the game but I'll be surprised if they are very, very dramatic," Granik said.
The league would like to address a drop in scoring this season, though the flow of the game was the main concern, not simply putting bigger numbers up, Stern and Granik said.
Asked what the repercussions would be to the league if its marquee team -- the defending champion Bulls -- were dismantled next season, the commissioner waxed philosophical.
"It's the soap opera part of what makes sports leagues so interesting to our fans," Stern said.

Bulls coach Phil Jackson's return is uncertain, with team management believed to be reluctant to pay him market value in this era of skyrocketing coaching salaries. The league's brightest star and top money generator, Michael Jordan, has said he will play for no one else.

In addition, perennial rumours about a trade of All-Star forward Scottie Pippen have cropped up, and the controversial rebounding champion Dennis Rodman may also be no longer welcome in the Windy City.
"I don't think it's anything you'd want to script but I believe it's just part of the game," said Stern.
When asked what he would be proudest of when his tenure ended, Stern cited the league's disproving of the idea that the NBA couldn't succeed because "America won't accept a black sport."

He noted that NBA players today are the highest paid athletes in the world, and said now perhaps the social issue to confront is the danger of children becoming "disproportionately focused" on the unrealistic idea of a future in the league.
Stern was also asked his feelings about the loud music played in NBA arenas these days. He said there had been a lowering of the volume this season -- to merely "earsplitting, deafening" levels.

Granik informed the media that the NBA checks decibel levels at all arenas. There are rules about when music can be played during games, and which music. Basically, music should not be used to disrupt visiting teams' offences.
"In addition to the profound issues of race, violence and social responsibility, we're dealing with things like pinwheels," Stern added.
Fans are often given objects to try to distract oponents at the free throw line, and there are ever-evolving rules about this, too.
